title: This man receives sinners (Luke 15:1–10)
hookLine: grumbling leads to three stories of lost things found

lines: A SNEER AT THE EDGE OF A CROWD.
cards: A sneer, overheard at the edge of a crowd. That's how Luke chapter fifteen begins. The chapter holds a lost sheep, a lost coin and a lost son, and it's easy to keep the stories and forget why Jesus told them.
They weren't bedtime stories. They were his answer to a complaint, and the complaint itself, meant as an insult, says something true about him.

teach.b: In the King James Bible: "Then drew near unto him all the publicans and sinners for to hear him. And the Pharisees and scribes murmured, saying, This man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them."
Publicans were tax collectors, and Luke sets them right beside the word sinners. Sharing a table, in that world, meant accepting someone.
So the worry was serious: what does it say about a teacher, about God, if he eats with these people?

The Greek word for murmured is a grumbling, muttering word. Some readers hear in it the same word family the old Greek version of Exodus uses when Israel grumbled in the wilderness. Jesus doesn't argue.
He tells three stories, and the stakes keep rising.

teach.h: ONE IN A HUNDRED, ONE IN TEN.
teach.b: A shepherd loses one sheep out of a hundred. A woman loses one coin out of ten. Tomorrow, a father loses one son out of two.

One percent, ten percent, half. And each of the first two ends not with the finding, but with a party. The shepherd calls his friends and neighbors: "Rejoice with me; for I have found my sheep which was lost."

The woman does the same: "Rejoice with me; for I have found the piece which I had lost." Then Jesus says it straight: "there is joy in the presence of the angels of God over one sinner that repenteth." Here's the twist.
The grumblers aren't the villains. They're being invited.

teach.h: EVERY STORY ENDS IN A PARTY.
teach.b: Every story ends with someone saying come and celebrate with me. When the lost come home, will you come to the party?
This man receives sinners. It was meant as an accusation. Luke keeps it as a description.

how: Christians read Luke 15 often, especially in Lent, and many churches mark returns with celebration: welcoming people back to communion, to membership, or into recovery communities that meet in church halls.

games.q: what's inside Luke 15:1–10 — tap the pairs.
p: one sheep out of a hundred

s: the stories of Luke 15 are told in answer to a complaint
"this man receiveth sinners, and eateth with them." the stories are his reply.
the first two stories end when the lost thing is found
they end with a party: "rejoice with me."
the stakes rise from one in a hundred, to one in ten, to one in two
a sheep, a coin, and then a son.

games.q: you're a teacher. tax collectors and sinners crowd in to hear you, and respected people grumble that you eat with them. what do you do?
o: tell three stories about lost things found, each ending in a party.
explain the rules for table fellowship.
games.why: Jesus doesn't argue. he tells of a lost sheep, a lost coin and a lost son, and each story invites the listeners to the celebration.

practice: Think of someone who has come back, to health, to sobriety, to the family table, to faith, to talking with you after a long silence, maybe in a way nobody marked.
Picture them clearly, notice if any part of you is still grumbling and let it be there, then try for a moment to feel the shepherd's joy instead. If you pray, give thanks for their return.

wordCard.voice: Publicans. Tax collectors who drew near to hear Jesus, and whose company with him made the Pharisees mutter that this man receives sinners.

orig.note: Greek: they were grumbling, muttering. the same word family describes Israel's grumbling in the Greek Exodus.

carryVoice: Your line: joy in heaven. The finding isn't the end; the party is. Day five hundred fifty-seven.
